facts.text: Named for the 19th century actor Edwin Forrest, who was born in Philadelphia.
Built at a cost of $2 million, with seating for 1,851.
Opened with a performance of The Red Robe.
Formerly the Electric Factory, renamed in October 2018 after a public naming contest.
Housed in a former General Electric Switchgear Plant building from 1916.
Sold to The Bowery Presents in September 2018.
Outdoor amphitheater and indoor theater complex on the Camden Waterfront, across the Delaware River from Philadelphia.
Formerly the Blockbuster-Sony Music Entertainment Centre, Tweeter Center, Susquehanna Bank Center and BB&T Pavilion.
Renamed Freedom Mortgage Pavilion in May 2022.
African-American theatre company founded in 1966 by John E. Allen Jr.
Moved in 1968 into the Edwin Forrest House on North Broad Street.
Pennsylvania's oldest African-American theatrical institution.
Includes a 299-seat proscenium theatre named for John E. Allen, Jr.
Hosts headline comedy shows and open mic nights.
Has two full-service bars and serves appetizers, sandwiches, entrees and desserts.
Built in 1886 and designed by architect Theophilus Parsons Chandler.
Located in a national historic landmark building that also houses the Tabernacle Church and the Christian Association.
The former church sanctuary was converted to a theater without altering the interior.
Opened in May 1929 and built between 1926 and 1932.
Houses the Curtis Organ, nearly 11,000 pipes, built for the 1926 Sesquicentennial Exposition and donated in 1928.
Restored and renovated in 1997 to 2000 by Venturi, Scott Brown & Associates.
Named for Kevin D. Marlo, an actor killed in the September 11 attacks on the World Trade Center.
Originally built in 1920 and restored and reopened in 2011 as part of Harcum College.
Available for community use such as meetings, music and theater performances.
Opened in January 2010 at William Penn Charter School.
A LEED Gold certified building with a green roof.
Named by the Kurtz family in memory of David L. Kurtz.
Lantern Theater Company was founded in 1994 by Charles McMahon and Michael Brophy.
The company has been in residence at St. Stephen's Theater since 1996.
Won the 2023 Barrymore Award for Outstanding Production of a Play.
Located in the Arts Bank, a historic bank building at 601 South Broad Street.
Named in memory of Philadelphia native Laurie Beechman, a singer and actress.
Located in The Drake building, with its entrance on Hicks Street between Spruce and Pine.
Shares the building with the Proscenium Theatre, home of InterAct Theatre Company.
Runs an after-school program for students.
Runs an acting camp.
A 424-seat proscenium theater.
Primary performance venue for the Theater, Music and Dance programs at Drexel University.
Stands at the corner of 33rd and Chestnut Streets, between the Creese Student Center and MacAlister Hall.
Formerly Verizon Hall, renamed Marian Anderson Hall in June 2024.
Home of the Philadelphia Orchestra, named for contralto and civil rights activist Marian Anderson.
Created by Tommy Joyner and Jamie Lokoff of MilkBoy Recording Studio.
Combines a restaurant, bar and cafe with an upstairs live music venue.
Has two full bars.
Originally the Sam S. Shubert Theatre, built by the Shubert brothers in 1918 to honor their late brother Sam.
Formerly the Merriam Theater, it was purchased by the Kimmel Center in November 2016.
Renamed for Alan B. Miller, a founding board member of the Kimmel Center.
Formed in 1923 as the Moment Musical Club by 19 members of the Falls Methodist Church.
Has used the Old Academy building in East Falls since 1932.
Grace Kelly began her acting career on its stage in 1942.
Opened in 1990 as the Ritz at the Bourse.
Philadelphia Film Society took over operation in 2021 and renovated all five theaters.
Opened in 1981 as the Budco Olde City 2 and became the Ritz East in 1999.
Philadelphia Film Society acquired the theater in 2022.
Founded in 1989 as the Red Heel Theatre.
Changed its name and purpose in 1993.
Renamed The Philadelphia Shakespeare Theatre in 2008 or 2009.
Founded in 1911, one of the oldest professional theater companies in the United States.
Building designed in 1912 by architect Amos W. Barnes as a dramatic school.
Murals were added in 1923 by artist Edith Emerson.
Bought by the Philadelphia Film Society in March 2015 and renamed Prince Theater.
Now operated by the Film Society as the Film Society Center.
Comedy club in Fishtown with about 300 seats, booked by Live Nation's House of Blues Entertainment division.
Has a lobby bar serving craft beers and pub grub, plus an outdoor patio.
Hosts local talent showcases and burlesque shows.
Two-floor, 500-person amphitheater inside the Comcast Technology Center.
Named for Comcast founder Ralph J. Roberts.
Hosts movie premieres, keynote speakers, talent panels and book signings.
